name: Five per cent of Pakistani Population has Hepatitis B

content.title: Five per cent of Pakistani Population has Hepatitis B
content.summary: A seminar on Hepatitis B was held at the Aga Khan University (AKU) on Monday, April 9, 2001. The seminar focused on many aspects of Hepatitis B prevention, including the proper vaccination of newborns, issues relating to adult vaccination.

media.alt: Five per cent of Pakistani Population has Hepatitis B

content.text: The seminar focused on many aspects of Hepatitis B prevention, including the proper vaccination of newborns, issues relating to adult vaccination, the best methods of vaccinating people, dealing with patients who do not respond to the vaccine, ensuring a safe supply of vaccine and preventing the use of unsafe needles.

Dr Saeed Hamid from the Department of Medicine, AKU, informed the audience of the prevalence of Hepatitis B in the country, which averages around 5% of the country's population. This amounts to more than 6 million people in Pakistan infected with Hepatitis B, that can potentially develop severe liver disease or liver cancer. Dr Wasim Jafri, from Department of Medicine, accentuated the importance of such seminars, which served to educate healthcare professionals on the latest aspects of these viral infections.

The keynote lecture was given by Dr Anthony Mounts from the WHO office, in Islamabad, who elaborated on the major global initiatives being taken for the control of Hepatitis B. Due to a highly-effective vaccine widely available, a number of global organisations have made the prevention of Hepatitis B their priority after the polio eradication programmes. The WHO has urged all countries to make Hepatitis B immunisation a part of the EPI programme, which is due to be launched in Pakistan later this year.

Dr Naseeruddin Mehmood from Department of Pediatrics, AKU, spoke on the recent development of combination vaccines, which incorporate the HB vaccine into the OPT vaccine, thus making it more convenient and cost-effective. Dr Wasim Jafri explained the necessity of vaccinating high-risk adult groups, which include healthcare workers. About 5% of the healthy population, he said, did not respond to the Hepatitis B vaccine. Dr Saeed Hamid pointed out the various strategies to increase the response to vaccination, including the use of correct size needles and the correct injection site.

Dr Arshad Altaf, from the Department of Community Health Sciences, stressed the need for safe and sterile injection techniques, as vaccinations are normally given by injections. He said Pakistan has one of the highest injection utilisation rates in the whole world, due to extensive use in medication as well as vaccination.
